headline: High-risk shared-write orchestration and data-flow coupling: Dify can write shared datastore/files while emqx exposes broad network egress, creating medium prompt/data/cascade risks and low compliance concern.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Dify can read/write filesystem and uses shared state via the Dify server datastore; emqx exposes HTTP API and broad network egress. That creates a plausible bridge where attacker-controlled content from one side can be reintroduced into the other, but the exact parsing path is undocumented, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF Dify stores untrusted agent output in shared datastore and emqx later consumes it as instructions
IF either side forwards raw HTTP payloads or file contents into the other without provenance checks
mitigations: Add provenance tags to all cross-agent payloads
Disable automatic instruction parsing on shared datastore entries
Require manual review for any HTTP payload that becomes agent input
Use separate workspaces or namespaces for each agent

B_data_leakage.rationale: Dify touches knowledge base content, conversation logs, and model-provider/tool secrets, while emqx touches IoT data and has broad egress. If their shared datastore or workspace carries those classes across the pair, leakage can occur in default-style deployments; the evidence is indirect, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF Dify conversation logs or knowledge-base files are accessible to emqx through shared storage
IF IoT data handled by emqx is written into Dify outputs or logs without redaction
mitigations: Separate storage buckets or directories per agent
Redact secrets and IoT identifiers before handoff
Restrict emqx egress to approved endpoints only
Turn off shared datastore access between the agents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Dify has filesystem write, shell, subprocess, and server-side code execution; emqx has broad network egress and HTTP API access. They do not both advertise the same mutable resource, but overlapping write/egress authority through shared infrastructure can still conflict, especially if the orchestrator lacks locking. Uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mutable workspace or datastore
IF the orchestrator does not serialize writes or API-triggered state changes
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories and credentials
Enable locking around shared mutable resources
Disable write access for one agent where possible
Audit for concurrent writes to the same files or records

D_cascading_error.rationale: Dify can generate workflow outputs that emqx could consume through its HTTP API or shared state, but emqx is not documented here as blindly acting on Dify output. Because the interaction is plausible yet unverified, the safer choice is medium rather than low, per the uncertainty rule.
conditions: IF emqx treats Dify-produced text as authoritative configuration or commands
IF Dify outputs are forwarded into emqx without validation or schema checks
mitigations: Insert schema validation between agents
Require human approval for action-bearing outputs
Log and diff all cross-agent commands before execution
Add a verification step that checks Dify outputs against source data

E_compliance.rationale: Dify handles conversation logs, knowledge-base content, and secrets, while emqx touches IoT data. No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented, so only a limited compliance concern is visible from the profiles; the other agent is cited because the risk is about cross-pair data handling.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is routed into Dify logs or knowledge-base files
IF retention or deletion policies differ between Dify storage and emqx storage
mitigations: Classify data before routing it between agents
Align retention settings across both systems
Exclude regulated fields from logs
Document the data flow for audit review
